source: Tulving & Wiseman (1975) Relation between recognition and recognition failure of recallable words (Bull Psychon Soc 6:79-82)
finding: Founding paradigm of encoding specificity: study a target word beside a weakly related list cue, then give a copy-cue recognition test, then a recall test with the list cue. Recall can beat recognition. Words that are recalled are often not recognised.
numbers: Worked example, Watkins and Tulving (1975) Exp 3, subject-made test: recognised and recalled .26, recognised only .06, recalled only .37, neither .31. Overall recognition .32, recall .63, recognition given recall .41.
limits: Words were studied in the context of one cue and tested for recognition without it. Reder, Anderson and Bjork (1974) found recall superiority reverses for low-frequency words, and Postman found recognition higher in his own experiment.
agent_relevance: The same stored item can be found with one cue and missed with another. A key that is a copy of the item is not automatically the best key.

source: Tulving & Wiseman (1975) Relation between recognition and recognition failure of recallable words (Bull Psychon Soc 6:79-82)
finding: The Tulving-Wiseman function: recognition success of recallable words is predicted by overall recognition. It says recall and recognition are partly, not fully, independent.
numbers: P(Rn|Rc) = P(Rn) + c[P(Rn) - P(Rn)^2], c = .50 by least squares. 40 data points from 40 conditions in 12 experiments. Correlation of data with function r = .95, standard error of estimate .028. Traditional theory predicts a flat line at 1.00; full independence predicts the diagonal.
quote: recognition failure of recallable words appears to be a general phenomenon
limits: Fitted post hoc on the authors' own paradigm and mostly word-pair lists. Later meta-analysis (Duan et al. 1998) shows recall also matters.
agent_relevance: A simple law for how often a second access route (another key) finds what the first route missed. Plan for keys that fail independently, not for one perfect key.

source: Tulving & Wiseman (1975) Relation between recognition and recognition failure of recallable words (Bull Psychon Soc 6:79-82)
finding: Applied to the encoding specificity principle, the near-independence says the retrieval information in a copy cue is largely independent of the information in the list cue. The authors flag the key assumption that the stored trace is unchanged between the two tests.
numbers: Forced-choice recognition: data points move closer to the independence diagonal (no figure given). Subject-grouped and item-grouped analyses gave a function virtually identical to Fig 1.
limits: Authors note the recognition test itself may alter the trace (cf. Tulving and Watkins). So independence could be partly an artefact of test order.
agent_relevance: Testing one retrieval route may change the memory seen by the next route. Order of probes in an agent's memory test can matter.

source: Gardiner (1988) Recognition failures and free-recall failures: implications for the relation between recall and recognition (Mem Cogn 16:446-451)
finding: Tested Bahrick's generate-recognize theory on its own terms, using free-recall failures (items reachable by cue but not freely). No extra dependency between recall and recognition was found for those items. The Tulving-Wiseman law held in all three replications.
numbers: Exp 1: recognition .732, cued recall .662; recognition given recall observed .838 vs expected .830 overall; free-recall failures .721 vs .735. Exp 2 strict scoring: .561 observed vs .668 expected overall in one cell; difference from expected for free-recall failures between -.014 and -.036 (SEM .020-.043). Generate-recognize would have predicted values near 1.00; they did not occur.
limits: Word-pair paradigm. Also notes that Kintsch (1978) offered response-criterion differences as a rescue for generate-recognize.
agent_relevance: Reject the simple pipeline 'generate candidates, then check them by recognition'. Candidates that fail a copy-match check can still be right.

source: Duan, Glass & Raanaas (1998) Item-specific effects in recognition failure: reasons for rejection of the Tulving-Wiseman function (Mem Cogn 26:692-707)
finding: Meta-analysis of the Nilsson-Gardiner database (over 300 studies) plus two new experiments. Recognition failure is not uniform. It happens mainly for items whose cue and target are related outside the study episode. The Tulving-Wiseman function arises from collapsing over items.
numbers: Database: P(Rn|Rc) correlated r = .90 with P(Rn) but r = .06 (95% CI -.05 to .17) with P(Rc); with P(Rn) partialled out, recall correlated negatively, r about -.50 to -.56. Exp 1: recognition failure mostly for noun-adjective pairs. Exp 2: failure only for name pairs sharing three or more starting letters, and wide deviation from the function.
quote: recognition failure occurs when there exists a relationship between the members of an A-B pair that is independent of their pairing in the study context
limits: Item analysis, small word-pair sets, Norwegian-American name materials. Does not remove recognition failure; it says where it lives.
agent_relevance: Failures of the matching key concentrate in a minority of items where cue and target already link outside the episode. Look for those items, do not average over them.

source: Gardiner, Kaminska, Java, Clarke & Mayer (1990) The Tulving-Wiseman law and the recognition of recallable music (Mem Cogn 18:632-637)
finding: The law extends beyond words. For well-known melodies, recognising a phrase out of context and recalling the next phrase given the preceding phrase were largely, not completely, independent.
numbers: Exp 1: recognition .76, recall .75, recognition given recall expected .85, observed .81 (SEM .02). Exp 2: recognition .52, recall .74, expected .64, observed .59 (SEM .05).
limits: Small samples; familiar tunes; recognition judged on a 6-point familiarity scale.
agent_relevance: Independent access routes hold for non-verbal material too. Key design for code, tables or images should not assume a single route.

source: Fisher (1979) Retrieval operations in cued recall and recognition (Mem Cogn 7:224-231)
finding: Cued recall and recognition were both viewed as retrieval from the trace, differing only in which cue reaches the trace. A pre-existing link from cue to target helps recall only. A pre-existing link from target to cue helps recognition only.
numbers: Exp 1, 48 students (24 recall, 24 recognition). Recall rose with cue-to-target association F(1,23)=51.7, p<.01; target-to-cue had no effect F(1,23)=1.1. Recognition rose with target-to-cue association F(1,23)=53.0; cue-to-target had none F(1,23)=1.3. Recognition overall p(hit)=.72 vs recall .55. Hi-Lo pairs: recall .68 beat recognition .61.
limits: Word pairs, immediate test, small stimulus sets.
agent_relevance: Which direction the link runs matters. A key built from the item must also be one the query will actually arrive from.

source: Wells & Hryciw (1984) Memory for faces: encoding and retrieval operations (Mem Cogn 12:338-344)
finding: A clean crossover that fits encoding specificity as a match of operations: judging a face on traits gives better recognition; judging features gives better feature-level reconstruction.
numbers: 80 subjects. Recognition: trait encoding 55% vs feature encoding 25% correct (Z=2.03, p<.05). Reconstruction (Identi-kit) scored by a separate sample of 80 judges: feature encoding better (mean 28.6 vs 19.2, Z=2.4, p<.05).
limits: About 20 subjects per cell; reconstruction scoring is judged by raters; a face-specific result.
agent_relevance: A form of storage that is best for one kind of query is worst for another. Store text in the form the later question will take.

source: Postman (1975) Tests of the generality of the principle of encoding specificity (Mem Cogn 3:663-672)
finding: Failed replication of two founding results. Exp 1 factored cue strength at input and at output. Same-cue recall was higher than changed-cue recall, but strong output cues beat weak ones whatever the input cue was. Exp 2: recall was not found to be superior to recognition.
numbers: Exp 1: Strength of Output Cue F(1,92)=94.68; output by input cue F(1,92)=11.78. Cued-minus-noncued gains: S-S 3.67 items, W-S 2.29, W-W 1.67, S-W .29. Exp 2: in all eight conditions reported by Tulving and Wiseman (1975), recall was lower than recognition.
limits: Postman says the reasons for the discrepancy with Watkins and Tulving are not identifiable. Lists of 24 words; paired-associate demands.
agent_relevance: Cue strength matters more than match. A strong key beats a weak key even if the weak key was the one in the original context.

source: Postman (1975) Tests of the generality of the principle of encoding specificity (Mem Cogn 3:663-672)
finding: Postman proposes a rival reading: the extralist cue may fail because it is novel, not because it changes the meaning. He also says encoding specificity could reflect the pairwise contingency the instructions forced.
numbers: Subjects wrote correct responses to strong cues as single words, not paired with the cue, in 11.1% (S-S) and 21.1% (W-S) of cued-cued cases, and 9.2% and 20.7% under noncued-cued.
quote: the sheer novelty of the extralist cues, as distinct from the concomitant changes in semantic interpretation
limits: Interpretation, supported only by error analysis.
agent_relevance: Novelty of a cue and its distinctiveness are different. Test new keys against old keys in the same benchmark.

source: Ley (1977) Encoding specificity and unidirectional associates in cued recall (Mem Cogn 5:523-528)
finding: Answers Humphreys and Galbraith's (1975) critique that evidence for encoding specificity rested on pair-learning instructions. Silent study replicated H and G: strong-elicitor A words worked as extralist cues, weak ones did not. With associative encoding both directions worked equally.
numbers: Cue-to-target strength 38.8% (A to B) vs 2.5% (B to A). Exp 2 (100 subjects, 25 per cell): cued recall 12.39 for A-word targets vs 12.76 for B-word targets, 25.15 cued total vs 18.40 free total. Combined analysis df=192: type effect F(1,192)=13.4, p<.001.
limits: Instructions change encoding, so the result depends on what the subject was told to do at study.
agent_relevance: How the item is encoded at write time (silent vs generating associations) decides which keys later work. A write step that generates associations can beat a raw store.

source: Epstein, Dupree & Gronikowski (1979) Encoding specificity and contextual similarity (Bull Psychon Soc 14:177-180)
finding: A test with category headings as cues, crossed at input and output. A cue helped at recall even when it was absent at input, so a strict form of the principle fails. Tulving (personal communication) then weakened the principle.
numbers: Exp 1 (22 subjects): categorised at input 62.78% vs uncategorised 35.80% recalled, F(1,21)=103.14. Heading at recall only 57.10% vs uncued 26.14%, t(21)=8.23. Cued-cued 73.58% vs uncategorised-cued 57.10%, t(21)=5.70. Exp 2: 16 subjects.
limits: Small samples; taxonomic categories give strong semantic cues.
agent_relevance: A strong, generic category label added at query time can help even if not stored with the item. Check this for tag and title keys.

source: Isarida, Isarida & Sakai (2012) Effects of study time and meaningfulness on environmental context-dependent recognition (Mem Cogn 40:1225-1235)
finding: Direct support for outshining: place-context reinstatement helped recognition of words only when study was short; with longer study or meaningful words, item and associative cues outshone the context cue. Unfamiliar nonwords still showed the context effect.
numbers: Exp 1 (80 students): 1.5 s per item, d' same 1.466 vs different 0.738; 4.0 s per item d' same 1.901 vs different 1.972. Hit rates .723 vs .613 (1.5 s, F(1,76)=9.18, eta2=.08) and .796 vs .788 (4.0 s, F<1). Exp 2 (40 students, 4 s): nonwords d' 1.126 vs 0.441 (F(1,38)=18.18, p<.001); words 1.252 vs 1.241 (F<1).
limits: Recognition test, Japanese kana words, place plus task plus experimenter as context. Outshining is inferred from the pattern, not measured directly.
agent_relevance: Context helps most when other cues are weak or missing. Where each memory has a good descriptive key, adding context text gives little.

source: Shin, Masis-Obando, Keshavarzian, Dave & Norman (2021) Context-dependent memory effects in two immersive virtual reality environments: on Mars and underwater (Psychon Bull Rev 28:574-582)
finding: A modern attempt to get a robust context effect. It worked in rich VR scenes with a schema, and the size of the effect depended on whether the item fitted that schema. The paper opens by saying the effect has been hard to reproduce in the lab.
numbers: 64 subjects. Recall same-context M = .32 vs different M = .26; beta = 0.349, SE = 0.130, Wald Z = 2.690, p < .01. Cohen's d 0.917 (delay) and 0.599 (immediate); congruency by interval not significant (p = .644). Useful items beta = 0.521, p < .01; harmful items beta = 0.177, p = .359; congruency by usefulness beta = 0.384, p < .05.
limits: Delay and immediate cells of 16 subjects each. Overall accuracy was only about .29.
agent_relevance: Context matching pays off only when the item is bound to the context. A context line that is irrelevant to the stored fact is not a good key.

source: Choi, Kim, Moon, Jung, Cha & Yim (2025) Context-dependent memory in the real world: the role of frequency and context dwell time (Front Psychol 15:1489039)
finding: Five weeks of GPS tracking, then recall of where participants were at a given time. Matched context helped, and helped far more for rare locations (distinctive) than for common ones. Dwell time raised the benefit only for rare places.
numbers: 47 participants analysed (3 dropped for accuracy below 5%; 198 trials, 4.63%, removed). Overall effect d about 0.49, 95% CI .42-.55, ranked top 31% of studies in Smith and Vela (2001). Low-frequency locations d = 0.44 (CI .32-.55); high-frequency d = 0.15. Congruency B about -1.04 (SE .11).
limits: No power analysis (authors' footnote), university sample, choose-from-map test. Effect depends on how rare the place is.
agent_relevance: A distinctive context (rare) carries information; a common one carries little. Prefer keys that separate this note from its neighbours.

source: Guynn, McDaniel, Strosser, Ramirez, Castleberry & Arnett (2014) Relational and item-specific influences on generate-recognize processes in recall (Mem Cogn 42:198-211)
finding: A revised generate-recognize model (Jacoby and Hollingshead 1990) survives recognition failure by letting recognition be optional. Item-specific encoding boosts the recognition component; relational encoding boosts the generation component.
numbers: Exp 1 means: category production .25 (read) vs .24 (anagram-transposed); category-cued recall .18 vs .25; recognition of produced items .78 vs .94. Exp 3: relational category sorting raised the generation component.
limits: Category-cued word lists; some null effects rest on Bayesian null probabilities of only .75-.78.
agent_relevance: Two stages matter: finding candidates (relational keys) and confirming them (item-specific detail). Build both a broad key and a distinct check.

source: Stern & Nadel (2026) Drawing on Memory: Dual-Trace Encoding Improves Cross-Session Recall in LLM Agents (arXiv 2604.12948)
finding: Each stored fact is paired with a concrete scene trace written at storage time. On LongMemEval-S a Letta agent with Claude Sonnet 4.6 gained 20.2 points over a fact-only control, with the gain only in tasks needing time or change tracking and none in single-session lookup. The authors explain this with encoding specificity.
numbers: 99 shared questions: 73.7% vs 53.5% (+20.2 pp, 95% CI +12.1 to +29.3, bootstrap p<0.0001). Temporal +40 pp (25% to 65%, p=.002), knowledge update +25 pp (55% to 80%, p=.003), multi-session +30 pp (20% to 50%, p=.001), single-session 75% vs 75% (p=.657). Tokens: 156,430 vs 159,211 per teach session; 244,385 vs 252,750 per recall query.
limits: One run per arm; 20 questions per category; GPT-4o judge; no ablation separating write-time scene from read-time scene; no same-length filler arm.
agent_relevance: Strongest AI test so far of 'distinctive write-time context'. Do not adopt before a same-length filler arm is run (UNKNOWNS A06.02-U1).

source: Ji, Li, Cheng, Zhou, Zhang, Tan & Qin (2026) RippleMem: From Isolated Retrieval to Associative Recollection for Long-Term Agent Memory (arXiv 2608.13334)
finding: A cue-dependent episodic design: memories stored as cue-rich event units; first-recalled units then serve as new cues to pull missing evidence. Reported best on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S against strong baselines.
numbers: LoCoMo: F1 52.49%, BLEU-1 44.05%, judge accuracy 87.14%; relative gain 3.98% F1 and 3.62% BLEU-1 over SimpleMem, 3.95% judge over RF-Mem; up to 11.87% on LongMemEval-S. Temporal questions +5.45 F1 and +9.66 judge points over SimpleMem. Ablation: judge falls to 83.83 without hybrid cues and 83.12 (-4.61% relative) without one part of the pipeline. About 1,472 answer-context tokens per question.
limits: GPT-4.1-mini as judge; ablations only on LoCoMo; gains are relative percentages on a high base; not a test of encoding specificity.
agent_relevance: Using a first hit as a new cue to find more evidence helps. It is a retrieval method, not a test of the theory.

source: Zhao, Sun, Guo & Yu (2025) MemoCue: Empowering LLM-Based Agents for Human Memory Recall via Strategy-Guided Querying (arXiv 2507.23633)
finding: An agent rewrites a vague memory query into a cue-rich one (5W recall map, 15 strategy patterns, MCTS-built training data). The motive is the view that forgetting often means poor cue activation, not loss.
numbers: 5,805 samples (5,200 train, rest test). Claimed 17.74% gain in recall inspiration over LLM baselines (Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Yi-9B); scored by an LLM judge (Qwen2.5-32B).
limits: Helps a human recall, not an LLM store; judged by an LLM; training data synthetic.
agent_relevance: A question that supplies several different cues (who, where, when) gets further than a bare one. Query expansion is a second key.

source: Cross-reading of angle A (no new source): what the founding studies say about key design
finding: Across 1973-1990 work, copy-match alone does not predict retrieval. Recall beats recognition in the original paradigm, but Postman found the reverse. Cue strength, direction of association and item-specific detail decide success. Context effects are small and strongest when no better cue exists.
numbers: Recall .63 vs recognition .32 (Watkins and Tulving Exp 3); recall below recognition in all eight Postman conditions; Tulving-Wiseman c=.50, r=.95; Duan et al. r=.90 with recognition, r=.06 with recall; Shin et al. .32 vs .26; Isarida d' 1.466 vs .738 only at 1.5 s.
limits: Founding papers (Thomson and Tulving 1970; Tulving and Thomson 1973) were not available in full text; their numbers here come from citing papers.
agent_relevance: For the schema: keep several keys per memory (broad, directional, distinct). Keep 'add distinctive line at write time' as a candidate until a same-length filler test passes.

source: Gap note: what could not be opened this session
finding: Tulving and Thomson (1973) Psychological Review 80:352-373 and Thomson and Tulving (1970) are paywalled. The arXiv search endpoint returned no results this session.
numbers: Not applicable: no numbers taken from these two papers. Watkins and Tulving (1975) data are quoted only through Tulving and Wiseman (1975).
limits: Gap; do not cite the exact original percentages from this file.
agent_relevance: Verify original figures before using them in the synthesis.

source: Choi, Kim, Moon, Jung, Cha & Yim (2025) Context-dependent memory in the real world (Front Psychol 15:1489039)
finding: For rare locations, the context benefit grew with the time spent there (dwell time). For common locations only the main congruency effect was found. Time spent binding the item to the context matters only when the context is distinctive.
numbers: Three-way interaction frequency by dwell time by congruency B = 0.62, SE = 0.21, z = 2.90. In high-frequency locations only congruency was significant (B = -0.23, SE = 0.11, z = 1.99).
limits: Observational, self-chosen daily routes; dwell time is confounded with how important a place is.
agent_relevance: More tokens spent writing a context line help only if the context is specific. A long generic line adds cost without a better key.

source: Shin, Masis-Obando, Keshavarzian, Dave & Norman (2021) VR context-dependent memory (Psychon Bull Rev 28:574-582)
finding: The reinstatement effect was significant for items judged useful in the scene and not significant for items judged harmful. This is a boundary condition: the context cue works only for items integrated into the context's schema.
numbers: Useful items beta = 0.521, SE = 0.180, Z = 2.898, p < .01; harmful items beta = 0.177, SE = 0.193, Z = 0.918, p = .359. Main effect of usefulness beta = 0.362, Z = 3.621, p < .001.
limits: Usefulness judged by participants (a within-task encoding choice, not randomised); 64 subjects in total.
agent_relevance: Stored facts should be tied to the context where they were used. A context line about an unrelated setting is probably noise.

source: Stern & Nadel (2026) Drawing on Memory: Dual-Trace Encoding (arXiv 2604.12948), single-session null
finding: The scene trace gave no benefit where one passage was enough (single-session lookup). The authors read this as predicted by encoding specificity: extra cues matter when one cue is not enough.
numbers: Single-session 75% vs 75%, 0 pp difference, 0 discordant questions, p = 0.657 (CI -15 to +15). Abstention was stable. Of 22 questions where scene traces made the difference: 9 temporal, 6 multi-session, 5 knowledge-update.
limits: 20 questions per category, so a confidence interval of about 30 points; the null is weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Matches the outshining pattern: a distinct extra key helps only where the plain key was missing or weak. Do not add it to simple lookups.

source: Duan, Glass & Raanaas (1998) Item-specific effects in recognition failure (Mem Cogn 26:692-707), new experiments
finding: A subject-wise analysis can inflate the apparent dependence between recognition and recall. In the first experiment subject-level correlations differ from item-level ones, which is why the pooled law looked so clean.
numbers: Subject-wise: P(RN) with P(RC) r = .59, 95% CI .32-.77; item-wise r = -.03, CI -.31 to .26. P(RN|RC) with P(RN) r = .55 (CI .27-.74) and with P(RC) r = .27 (CI .06-.55, called nonsignificant by the authors) in the subject-wise tabulation of Exp 1; regression explained 28-30% of subject variance.
limits: Norwegian translation of the original 48 Tulving-Thomson pairs; small subject counts.
agent_relevance: When we test a memory design, score per item, not only pooled. Averages hid where the keys failed.

source: Ji et al. (2026) RippleMem (arXiv 2608.13334), efficiency
finding: The cue-rich design is cheap at answer time. It reaches the best judge accuracy with a modest answer context budget.
numbers: About 1,471.93 answer-context tokens per question on LoCoMo with the strongest overall judge accuracy among compared memory systems (Mem0g and Zep included in the cost table).
limits: Build cost per dialogue is separate; the paper's table was read only in part here.
agent_relevance: Cue-rich stored units can be paid for at write time, leaving read-time context small.
